name: Orizon
tagline: Upload an interface screenshot, get an AI-generated UX critique with prioritized fixes.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core mechanic here is a vision model plus a good heuristics rubric, and a coding agent can wire that up in an afternoon. What you get is genuinely useful: drop in a screenshot, receive findings grouped by severity, export a checklist. What you will not get is the tuned prompt chain, the design-system awareness, or the Figma side of the workflow, and your version's advice will be blander until you spend real time on the rubric. It also depends on a hosted model API, so this is not a self-contained build. Call it a weekend project that covers most of the value for one person reviewing their own screens.
coreLoopDIY: Drag in a screenshot, send it to a vision model with a fixed UX heuristics rubric, and render the returned findings as a severity-ranked report you can export.
requirements: An OpenAI or Anthropic API key with vision access
Node 20 and a local SQLite file
Willingness to iterate on the rubric prompt, which is where all the quality lives
whatYouLose: Prompt tuning done across thousands of real interfaces, so your critiques read more generic
Figma or browser plugin ingestion instead of manual screenshot dragging
Any notion of your design system, so fixes ignore your tokens and components
Shareable review links and comment threads for handing findings to someone else
Batch crawling of a whole site or flow instead of one screen at a time
moatNotes: The defensible part is taste encoded in prompts plus the plugin plumbing, not the model call itself.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a critique tool is only worth anything if the critique is sharp, and sharpness comes from someone having already argued with the model for months about what a useful finding looks like. Paying also buys the boring parts: the plugin that grabs frames without you screenshotting them, links you can paste into a ticket, and output consistent enough to show a client. A homegrown version is fine for auditing your own landing page and unconvincing the moment another human reads it.
notes: The model does the seeing; the rubric does the thinking, and the rubric is the part you have to earn.
prompt:
Build a local AI UX review tool called ScreenCritic. Run it on my machine only.
Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, better-sqlite3 for storage, no auth, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.
Core loop: I drag a screenshot onto the page (or paste an image URL), pick a context from a fixed list (marketing landing page, signup or checkout flow, app dashboard, mobile screen), and get a structured critique back.
Server route sends the image to a vision model using OPENAI_API_KEY from .env. Read the model name from .env too, default to a current vision-capable model. If the key is missing, fail with a clear message, do not silently mock.
Keep the entire review prompt in one editable file at prompts/rubric.ts so I can tune it without touching app code.
Rubric sections: visual hierarchy, contrast and readability, affordance clarity, form and input friction, copy clarity, mobile layout risk, accessibility red flags.
Force strict JSON output: an array of findings, each with area, severity (1 low to 3 blocking), what, why, fix. Plus an overall summary string and exactly three priority fixes. Validate with zod and retry once on parse failure.
Render findings grouped by severity, worst first, collapsible, with the screenshot pinned beside them. If the model returns bounding boxes, draw them over the image; if not, skip markers entirely rather than faking them.
Store every review in SQLite: image file on disk under ./uploads, findings as JSON, context, model name, timestamp, cost estimate if the API returns usage.
History page listing past reviews with thumbnails, filterable by context.
Export a single review as Markdown checklist, with severity, fix, and a checkbox per finding.
Batch mode: drop up to 10 images, queue them sequentially, show per-image status, do not fire 10 parallel calls.
Out of scope, do not build: Figma or browser plugins, redesign generation, user accounts, shareable public links, heatmaps, real user session data, design system or token awareness, hosted deployment config.
Include a README with setup steps, a .env.example, and a seed script that inserts one fake review so the history page is not empty on first run.
Keep it to one npm install and npm run dev. No Docker.
